payload.folded:
SP1 - THE DECRYPTION ROUND TRIP: 6/6, run-e8599b7b7d2a. Ran under Node's globalThis.crypto.subtle, which IS the browser's Web Crypto implementation, so the browser leg is proven without a browser. What it CONFIRMED upstream: se.adr-brief-encrypted-fragment-key survives contact - a 20k brief seals to a 26KB payload, round-trips exactly, and the three silent-corruption paths all throw rather than returning garbage (wrong key, tampered ciphertext, wrong tag position). GCM authenticates, so a corrupted brief cannot render as a plausible one. What it CHANGED upstream: TWO details are now contract, not preference, and both were wrong in my own earlier throwaway probe. (a) THE PAYLOAD LAYOUT is iv(12) | tag(16) | ciphertext, stated once and honoured on both sides - Node hands the tag back separately while Web Crypto demands it appended to the ciphertext, so the opener must REJOIN as ct||tag. My probe script had this scrambled and would have shipped a page that never decrypts while every server-side check stayed green - which is precisely the failure class this spike existed to catch. (b) THE KEY IS base64url, not base64: a plain-base64 key carries + / and = into a URL fragment, and my probe put exactly that in the link. Neither of these reopens a gate; both sharpen a ruled decision into an implementable contract.

SP2 - THE WAIT SIGNAL: answered, and better than the design assumed. The question was whether the announce path can know that the run is about to wait for the owner. Reading the shipped lane: it CANNOT, by construction - announceOffer is driven by a 3-second timer in the board process (bin/se-board.ts phoneTick) that sees only 'an offer exists' and publishes on the edge. A timer cannot know the run's intent, which is the structural reason the shipped lane cannot implement the owner's corrected rule at all - not a tuning problem, a wrong-caller problem. THE ANSWER: the park is ALREADY AN EXPLICIT TOOL CALL. se_wait { condition: { kind: 'offer' } } is the declared wait lane (engine/wait.ts), and the machine recommends it the moment a gate is offered. An agent that will self-bless calls se_gate_bless immediately and never waits; an agent that will park for the owner calls se_wait. So the signal needs no inference, no timeout heuristic and no configuration: THE ACT OF WAITING IS ITSELF THE TRIGGER. This is a whitelist by construction - one named act publishes, everything else does not - rather than a rule that tries to detect unattendedness.

RIPPLE, stated rather than assumed: this MOVES the announce trigger from E5 (the board hook) to the park seam, while leaving the element set and every allocation intact - E3 still owns 'summon the owner', it is simply invoked by the run that parks instead of by a poller that noticed. I considered whether this reopens gate_architecture and ruled that it does not: M5 specified that E3 fires regardless of E2, and left its trigger unspecified, so the spike SETTLES an open detail rather than contradicting a ruled one. The board keeps polling ANSWERS on its timer - a tap must still land while the agent's turn is over - so E4's placement is unchanged. One consequence worth naming now: an agent that parks by ending its turn WITHOUT calling se_wait announces nothing. That is a real hole and it is being closed visibly rather than by heuristic - the offer records whether it was announced, so an un-announced live offer is legible on the board instead of silently unsent.
payload.promotions:
PROMOTED INTO THE BUILD, verbatim:

1. SP1's seal/open pair - the AES-256-GCM sealing side and the byte-exact opening side, including the iv|tag|ct layout, the ct||tag rejoin, and base64url for the fragment key. This is proven code, not a sketch; it enters engine/brief.ts unchanged in substance.
2. SP1's four negative checks (wrong key, tampered ciphertext, wrong tag position, url-safe charset) - promoted as PERMANENT TESTS, not as spike residue. They are the only thing standing between a shipped brief and a page that silently fails to decrypt.
3. SP2's finding that se_wait is the trigger - promoted as the build's central wiring decision and as the R9 acceptance check: publish iff the run parks on the offer.

NOT PROMOTED, deliberately: the throwaway probe script (jobs tmp) - it carried both crypto defects SP1 found and must not be mistaken for a reference; SP1's own script supersedes it. Nothing from either spike is carried as 'to be cleaned up later'.

OUT-OF-BAND FINDING, filed not fixed: note-65857e4bd6e6. Chasing SP2 I called se_file_search with the wrong argument name; instead of refusing a missing required arg, the tool coerced undefined and searched the product for the literal word 'undefined', returning a page of real hits that answered nothing. I believed it and drew a wrong conclusion (drained as note-9de6f8eaac65). The defect generalizes past this tool: required args are not enforced at dispatch, so any tool can be called with wrong arg names and will answer confidently on garbage. That is the whitelist-guard law applied to arguments, and it is exactly the expensive failure class - not an error, a confident wrong answer. Routed to i9; it does not block this build.
